hints.title: Write the sum in terms of n
hints.body: Write all four consecutive integers starting with n, then add them.
hints.recap: Translate a statement about integers into algebra before trying to prove it.
hints.pitfall: Include the starting integer and exactly three more.

recall.reminder: Translate a statement about integers into algebra before trying to prove it.

hints.title: Check the factors of six
hints.body: A number is divisible by six exactly when it is divisible by both two and three. Apply both tests to your sum.
hints.recap: Cover every possible remainder to prove a divisibility claim.
hints.pitfall: A few successful examples do not prove the condition for every n.
hints.pause: Use the possible remainders of n to find and prove the complete condition.

recall.reminder: Cover every possible remainder to prove a divisibility claim.

solution:
The sum is 4n+6. For n=3k this is 6(2k+1), a multiple of 6. For the other two residue classes it is 12k+10 or 12k+14, neither divisible by 3.

Thus the sum is a multiple of 6 exactly when n is a multiple of 3. Answer C.
